name: Umar Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. To start, what's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a wheel loader, a big front-end loader, on the stockpiles at the phosphate mine at Dunmore Flats. The trucks dump ore on the run-of-mine pad, that's the big flat area before the crusher, and I feed the crusher and blend the piles so the plant gets an even grade.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you interested after all these years?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The blending, honestly, it's like cooking with a thousand-tonne spoon. I keep my own spreadsheet of tonnes per hour and fuel burn, and every night I ask a chatbot to help me find patterns in it, which my supervisor finds hilarious. What wears me out is the dust and the noise. On weekends I fly a drone for a real estate agent in town, photos of houses, which keeps me sane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a good tool, not a miracle. I'd probably post a joke in the site group chat about the robots not turning up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed. I'm curious, I want to see what it can do. But for my bank balance and my retirement plan, it's all fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, keep my spreadsheet, keep the drone work. I'd probably ask to try the autonomous loader trial anyway, just to learn it. Zsofia and I would keep putting money aside for the house in the hills we want at sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a tiny bit bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the autonomous loader trial at your mine look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's one loader on the far stockpile with sensors all over it like a hedgehog. It works great on a sunny day and gets confused in the dust. I've been asking to sit with the engineers who run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the drone work bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three or four hundred a month, depending on the market. It's not much, but it's mine. And it's taught me more about cameras and software than ten years of company training.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool, not a miracle, and post a joke in the site group chat about the robots not turning up.
S0.think: Privately I'd be a little disappointed, because I'm curious to see what it can do. For my money and retirement plan, though, it's all fine.
S0.do: Carries on with his work, his own performance spreadsheet and weekend drone photography. Asks to try the autonomous loader trial for the learning and keeps saving for a house in the hills at sixty-two.
S0.quote: It's one loader on the far stockpile with sensors all over it like a hedgehog.
S0.fieldNote: Umar is calm and almost disappointed at the plateau, since he enjoys new tools for their own sake. His small drone business already gives him a second income and a technical hobby. He is the only person at his site asking to sit with the automation engineers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening anyway, so let's be in the room when they plan it. I wouldn't take the union's side or the bosses' side automatically, I'd want to see the actual deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a loader on a stockpile goes remote early, maybe in three or four years. But I think there's a job for someone who knows the stockpiles and knows the software. I'd like to be that person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the mine manager in the first month and volunteer for the automation team, even on the same pay. I'd do an online course in industrial automation at night. I'd also grow the drone work, maybe get a licence for surveying stockpiles, which mines actually pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. I like a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd volunteer for the team that might automate your own job. How do your workmates see that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them think I'm a traitor, not to my face but I hear it. My answer is that the machine's coming either way, and I'd rather it's set up by someone who knows where the soft ground is. Not all of them buy that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Zsofia think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a primary teacher, so she's seen every new gadget come through a classroom. She'd tell me to go for it, but not to promise the mine my weekends. She's protective of the weekends.

S1.say: I'd say it's happening anyway, so let's be in the room when it's planned. I wouldn't side automatically with the union or the bosses; I'd want to see the actual deal.
S1.think: Privately I think stockpile loading goes remote in three or four years. I think there's a job for someone who knows the stockpiles and the software, and I'd like to be that person.
S1.do: Volunteers for the mine's automation team in the first month, even on the same pay, and studies industrial automation online at night. Grows his drone work towards a licence for surveying stockpiles.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, since he likes a project.
S1.quote: I'd rather it's set up by someone who knows where the soft ground is.
S1.fieldNote: Umar would help automate his own job, and he's aware some colleagues see that as betrayal. He frames it as practical: the machines come either way. His drone hobby gives him a credible route into mine surveying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, me included. I'd probably say the government needs a short-term fix for older workers and stop there, I don't like big promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being curious doesn't save me this time. If AI can plan the blend and robots can drive the loader, my spreadsheet is a hobby. And drones will fly themselves, so the side work goes too. Two years puts me at sixty with about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to grab one of the few human jobs left on the automation side, commissioning or checking the machines, for as long as it lasts. We'd stop putting money towards the house in the hills and hold onto the cash instead. I'd use the drone money while it lasts and look at whether the house deposit should go into something that gains from all this, but carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My head's still working, which helps, but my gut doesn't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'something that gains from all this'. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shares in the companies making the robots, maybe, but only a small slice. I'm not a gambler with the house money. It's more that I'd rather own a piece of the thing than just watch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does two years of warning change your plans, compared with a slower version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, being an early adopter buys me maybe one extra year of work. With more time it could buy me the rest of my career. The head start is the same size, but the race is shorter.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast for anyone, including me, and that the government needs a short-term fix for older workers. I don't like big promises, so I'd stop there.
S2.think: Privately being curious doesn't save me if AI plans the blend and robots drive the loader and the drones. Two years puts me at sixty with about four months saved.
S2.do: Tries to grab one of the few human commissioning or checking jobs on the automation side for as long as it lasts. Pauses saving for the house in the hills, keeps cash, and considers moving a small slice of savings into shares of robot makers.
S2.feel: Anxious, with his mind still working but his gut uneasy.
S2.quote: The head start is the same size, but the race is shorter.
S2.fieldNote: Umar is honest that adaptability buys him little when everything changes in two years. His instinct is to own a small piece of the change rather than only suffer it, but he is cautious with the house money. His centrist dislike of big promises shows even here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable if you start now. I'd be the one at the tea break telling people to do the automation course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to sixty-three, a year past my plan. I think I'd spend most of it on the automation side and come out fine. I'm a little uneasy about the last year or two, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd get on the automation team, finish the online course, and get the drone surveying licence. I'd put a bit of savings into robot-maker shares, small, and keep the house plan going. I'd aim to stop at sixty-two on schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, but mostly I'd feel lucky to like this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you try to bring along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, who runs the other loader. He's fifty-five and good with his hands, terrible with a phone. I'd sit with him on the course, and I'd probably fail at that, but I'd try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nora's twenty-four and studying law, so I'd tell her to learn the AI tools hard and fast. Our son Ádám sells cars, and I'd tell him people will still want a person to argue the price with, for a while.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight but workable if you start now. I'd be the one at the tea break telling people to do the automation course.
S3.think: Privately five years takes me a year past my plan, and I think I'd spend most of it on the automation side and come out fine. I'm a little uneasy about the last year or two.
S3.do: Joins the automation team this year, finishes the online course and gets a drone surveying licence. Puts a small amount into shares of robot makers, keeps saving for the house and aims to stop at sixty-two.
S3.feel: Uneasy at the edges but mostly lucky to enjoy the new technology.
S3.quote: He's fifty-five and good with his hands, terrible with a phone.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Umar's adaptability pays off and he expects to work on the automation side until his planned exit. He wants to bring a less tech-friendly colleague along, while admitting it may not work. He tailors advice to each of his kids' jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody has an excuse. I'd share good courses and practical advice online, not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd retire at sixty-two in the hills and watch it with interest. I might even miss being in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what I'd do anyway: join the automation team, keep the drones, save for the house. I'd put a small regular amount into robot-maker shares every month. And I'd stop at sixty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly curious. I'd want to see how it turns out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in retirement if the world was full of robots doing work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fly drones over the hills for fun instead of money. Help Zsofia with her vegetable patch. Maybe teach older guys at the community centre how to use these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything in the ten-year version worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the young ones in Dunmore Flats find something to do. The mine's the main employer. Ten years is enough to fix that, but only if someone actually does it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody has an excuse. I'd share good courses and practical advice online rather than panic.
S4.think: Privately it's fine, because I'd retire at sixty-two in the hills and watch it with interest. I might even miss being in the middle of it.
S4.do: Joins the automation team, keeps the drone work and saves for the house as planned. Puts a small monthly amount into robot-maker shares and retires at sixty-two.
S4.feel: Calm and curious about how it turns out.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to fix that, but only if someone actually does it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years leaves Umar comfortable, curious and planning to teach older people at the community centre. He invests steadily rather than boldly. His one worry is jobs for young people in a one-employer town.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my head start doesn't count for much. What would help is short, paid training for older workers on the automation side and a way to take some retirement money early. Practical things, not slogans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask people what they'd miss, not just what they'd lose. I'd miss the smell of the ore after rain. No spreadsheet gives you that.

headlineQuote: I'd miss the smell of the ore after rain. No spreadsheet gives you that.
portrait: Umar Varga is a 58-year-old wheel loader operator who blends the stockpiles at a phosphate mine in Dunmore Flats, keeps his own performance spreadsheet, uses a chatbot every day and flies a drone for a real estate agent at weekends. He is pragmatic and doesn't side automatically with bosses or the union. He is calm under the plateau and steady change, when he'd volunteer to help automate his own job, but anxious if AGI arrives in two years because his head start counts for little. With five or ten years he expects to work on the automation side, invest a little in robot makers and retire to the hills at sixty-two.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his early start with technology would buy him very little time.
whatWouldHelp: Short, paid training for older workers on the automation side and a way to take some retirement money early.
